report:
## Conclusion

Yes — the evidence strongly supports that EMDR therapy alleviates PTSD symptoms in adults. Multiple systematic reviews and meta-analyses find EMDR produces significant, moderate-to-large reductions in PTSD symptoms compared to waitlist or no-treatment controls, and it performs comparably to trauma-focused cognitive-behavioral therapy (TF-CBT), such as prolonged exposure and cognitive processing therapy, which are also first-line treatments (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_movement_desensitization_and_reprocessing; pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37882423/). A 2023 meta-analysis specifically evaluating EMDR's efficacy for PTSD confirmed clinically meaningful symptom reduction, and a 2023 review by Yunitri and colleagues (98 RCTs, ~5,567 participants) found EMDR among the treatments with the strongest long-term effects on PTSD outcomes (pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37882423/).

This is reflected in major clinical guidelines: the American Psychological Association's 2017 PTSD treatment guideline includes EMDR as a recommended treatment (conditional recommendation, reflecting good but not the very highest-tier evidence relative to some CBT variants), and the World Health Organization's 2013 guidance on mental health care after trauma explicitly recommends EMDR alongside trauma-focused CBT as effective interventions (apa.org/ptsd-guideline/treatments/eye-movement-reprocessing; who.int/news/item/06-08-2013-who-releases-guidance-on-mental-health-care-after-trauma).

Comparative studies suggest EMDR and TF-CBT are broadly equivalent in efficacy, though EMDR sometimes shows faster symptom relief since it typically doesn't require detailed verbal disclosure of trauma or homework, making it appealing for some patients (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK73148/).

**Bottom line:** EMDR is a well-supported, evidence-based treatment that effectively reduces PTSD symptoms, with efficacy comparable to established trauma-focused CBT approaches, and is endorsed by both APA and WHO guidelines.
